Push, reactivity and concurrency

Source: vignettes/reactivity.Rmd
reactivity.Rmd

A spigot page can exchange data with R in three ways. Most apps need only the first.

Channel Direction Use it for R side Page side
HTTP page → R → page Queries, commands, forms, loading data plumber endpoints spigot.get(), spigot.post(), …
Push R → page Live updates, progress, events another tab caused spigot_emit(), spigot_broadcast() spigot.on()
Bridge HTTP → reactive graph An API call that should update reactive code in the server function spigot_trigger() nothing: spigot.js handles it

Rules of thumb:

  • Start with HTTP. A page asks; R answers. Shiny hosts the app and gives each tab a session, and that is all most apps need from it.
  • Push when R knows something the page did not ask for: another user changed the data, a long job made progress, a timer fired.
  • Use the bridge only when the server function owns the view: Shiny outputs, or reactive code that should run when an endpoint is called. It is optional; nothing else in spigot depends on it.

The live example uses all three. Run it with spigot::run_example("live") and open it in two tabs.

Push: spigot_emit() and spigot_broadcast()

spigot_emit(session, event, data) sends an event to one tab: the session of the request, from spigot_session(req) in an endpoint, or the session of a server function. spigot_broadcast(event, data) sends it to every open tab. The page listens with spigot.on():

const stop = spigot.on("cart:changed", (cart, event) => renderCart(cart));
// later, if needed:
stop();
#* @post /cart/add
function(req, sku) {
  s <- spigot::spigot_session(req)
  cart <- add_to_cart(s$userData$cart_id, sku)
  spigot::spigot_emit(s, "cart:changed", cart)
  cart
}

data is serialised with spigot_json(), so it arrives in the page in the same shape as an API reply. Events travel over the tab’s Shiny websocket.

spigot_broadcast() takes except, sessions to skip, and filter, a function of a session that returns TRUE to send to it. Together they cover “tell everyone else” and rooms:

#* @post /chat/say
function(req, text) {
  s <- spigot::spigot_session(req)
  room <- s$userData$room
  spigot::spigot_broadcast("chat:message", list(room = room, text = text),
    except = s, filter = function(x) identical(x$userData$room, room))
}

Things to know about push:

  • A push can beat the reply. R sends an event as soon as spigot_emit() is called, while the endpoint is still running, so the page can receive it before the HTTP reply to the same request. Do not write page code that assumes the reply comes first. The live example keeps the highest count it has seen, whichever message carries it.
  • No replay. Events that arrive before the page calls spigot.on() for them are dropped. Register listeners when the script loads, and load the current state over HTTP.
  • One R process. spigot_broadcast() reaches the open tabs served by this R process. If the server runs several processes for one app, tabs in other processes do not get the event. Pushing across processes needs an outside relay, such as Redis or Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY, and spigot does not provide one.
  • Push from the app’s process: an endpoint, an observer, a later::later() callback. A future worker is another R process and has no sessions. Emit from the promise’s then(), which runs in the app’s process.

The bridge: spigot_trigger()

spigot_trigger(session, name, value) sets input[[name]] in a tab’s session, so the server function’s reactive code runs as if the page had changed an input:

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  mine <- reactiveVal(0L)
  observeEvent(input$clicked, mine(mine() + input$clicked))
  output$mine <- renderText(mine())
}

A hand-written page shows a Shiny output with an element that has the output’s id and class, here <div id="mine" class="shiny-text-output"></div>. Shiny binds it as it would a textOutput(). Other outputs use their own classes: shiny-html-output for uiOutput(), shiny-plot-output for plotOutput(), and so on.

How it behaves:

  • The value never leaves R. spigot keeps value in the session and sends the page only an id; the page sets the input to the id and spigot swaps the value back in. So input[[name]] is identical() to value: data frames, factors, dates and NA arrive unchanged. The value stays in the session until the page sends the id back, or the session ends.
  • It runs after the endpoint returns, in Shiny’s normal reactive flush, and only if the tab is open and has loaded spigot.js (every spigot page has). It takes one more trip over the websocket, about as long as any Shiny input change.
  • Every trigger fires. Observers run even when the value equals the last one.
  • Modules. Called with a module’s session, name is namespaced like the module’s own inputs.

If you only need the page to show new data, return it or push it; there is no need to go through the reactive graph.

The live example

app.R keeps the shared state in an environment that the endpoints and the server function both see, and broadcasts the number of open tabs when one opens or closes:

# spigot "live" example: a counter shared by every open tab. It uses all three
# channels between a page and R:
#
# * HTTP: the page reads and changes the count with spigot.get() and
#   spigot.post() (api.R).
# * Push: R sends every open tab the new count with spigot_broadcast(), and
#   the page listens with spigot.on().
# * Bridge: the endpoint also sets an input of the calling tab with
#   spigot_trigger(), so that tab's server function updates a Shiny output
#   on the page.
#
# Run it with spigot::run_example("live"), then open the page in a second tab.
library(shiny)
library(spigot)

# State shared by every tab. It lives in this R process, so the endpoints in
# api.R (evaluated in this environment) and the server function see the same
# values.
shared <- new.env()
shared$count <- 0L
shared$tabs <- 0L

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  # A tab opened or closed: tell every tab how many are open.
  shared$tabs <- shared$tabs + 1L
  spigot_broadcast("tabs", list(tabs = shared$tabs))
  session$onSessionEnded(function() {
    shared$tabs <- shared$tabs - 1L
    spigot_broadcast("tabs", list(tabs = shared$tabs))
  })

  # This tab's own clicks. The increment endpoint sets input$clicked with
  # spigot_trigger(); the page shows output$mine in an element with the
  # class "shiny-text-output".
  mine <- reactiveVal(0L)
  observeEvent(input$clicked, mine(mine() + input$clicked))
  output$mine <- renderText(mine())
}

spigot_app(
  pages = spigot_page("index.html"),
  server = server,
  api = "api.R"
)

The increment endpoint uses all three channels: the reply carries the new count, a broadcast tells every tab, and a trigger tells the calling tab’s server function.

# The example's API. `shared` is defined in app.R: spigot_app() evaluates this
# file in app.R's environment.

#* The count and the number of open tabs. A plain HTTP read.
#* @get /state
function() {
  list(count = shared$count, tabs = shared$tabs)
}

#* Add `by` (1 to 10) to the count, tell every tab, and tell this tab's
#* server function.
#* @post /increment
function(req, res, by = 1) {
  by <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(by))
  if (length(by) != 1 || is.na(by) || by < 1 || by > 10) {
    res$status <- 400L
    return(list(error = "by must be a whole number from 1 to 10"))
  }
  shared$count <- shared$count + by

  # Push: every open tab, this one included, gets the new count.
  spigot_broadcast("count", list(count = shared$count, by = by))
  # Bridge: this tab's server function sees input$clicked change.
  spigot_trigger(spigot_session(req), "clicked", by)

  list(count = shared$count)
}

The page’s script listens for both events, loads the current state once, and calls the API from its buttons:

// The page's only script. spigot_app() adds spigot.js, which defines spigot.get(),
// spigot.post() and spigot.on().

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);

// The count only goes up, so show the highest value seen. A reply and a push
// can arrive in either order: R sends the push while the endpoint runs, so it
// can reach the page before the reply to the same request.
let shown = -1;
function showCount(n) {
  if (n <= shown) return;
  shown = n;
  $("count").textContent = n;
}

const lines = [];
function log(line) {
  lines.push(`${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}  ${line}`);
  $("log").textContent = lines.slice(-10).join("\n");
}

// Push: R calls spigot_broadcast() when the count changes or a tab opens or closes.
spigot.on("count", (msg) => {
  showCount(msg.count);
  log(`push  count: ${msg.count} (+${msg.by})`);
});

// The number of tabs goes down as well as up, so "highest seen" does not work
// for it. Once one push has arrived, every later change arrives as a push too,
// and a reply that lands after it may be older, so the reply is ignored.
let tabsPushed = false;
spigot.on("tabs", (msg) => {
  tabsPushed = true;
  $("tabs").textContent = msg.tabs;
  log(`push  tabs: ${msg.tabs}`);
});

// HTTP: read the current state once. spigot.get() waits for the Shiny session.
spigot.get("state").then((s) => {
  showCount(s.count);
  if (!tabsPushed) $("tabs").textContent = s.tabs;
});

async function add(by) {
  try {
    const reply = await spigot.post("increment", { by });
    showCount(reply.count);
    log(`reply count: ${reply.count}`);
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof spigot.SpigotError)) throw err;
    log(`reply ${err.status}: ${err.message}`);
  }
}

$("plus-one").addEventListener("click", () => add(1));
$("plus-five").addEventListener("click", () => add(5));
$("plus-bad").addEventListener("click", () => add(11));

Concurrency

A Shiny app runs in one R process with one thread. While an endpoint runs, nothing else in that process does: no other request, no other tab’s reactive code, no pushes. A query that takes two seconds makes every tab wait two seconds.

For anything slower than about 100 ms:

  • Return a promise. spigot replies when it resolves, and the process serves other requests meanwhile. promises::future_promise() runs the work in a future worker; mirai works too. The site example’s fit endpoint is a complete example.

    #* @post /report
function(req, month) {
  s <- spigot::spigot_session(req)
  promises::future_promise({
    build_report(month)          # runs in a worker
  }) |>
    promises::then(function(report) {
      # back in the app's process: sessions and push work here
      spigot::spigot_emit(s, "report:ready", list(month = month))
      report
    })
}

  • Send the worker what it needs. A worker is another R process: it has no sessions and none of the app’s in-memory state. Pass data in, and use the result in then().

  • Wait without blocking. To wait for something, resolve a promise from later::later() instead of calling Sys.sleep(). The minimal example’s /slow endpoint does this.

  • Give the page a timeout. spigot.get(path, query, {timeout: 5000}) rejects with a SpigotError whose status is 0 if no reply arrives within five seconds, and aborts the request.
